name: Grace Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Grace, thanks for doing this. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. Your name won't be attached to anything you say. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Fernleaf, a small worker co-op that does eco retrofits on old terraced houses, so that means insulating walls, fitting timber windows and putting wood-fibre boards on the inside of cold brick. I'm a first-year carpenter, so I'm the one cutting boards and fixing battens while Tomasz, our lead carpenter, does the tricky window openings. Every morning on the bus I ask an AI app to turn yesterday's measurements into a cut list, and Tomasz checks it. I love it, but my measuring still lets me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to carpentry?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I left school at sixteen, worked in cafés, then co-ran a little vegan café for five years. When we sold it, I came out with a decent lump that's sitting in an index fund, and I decided I wanted to make things that last longer than a flat white. Noor, my girlfriend, is a freelance graphic designer, so between us we're fine for money, just very different kinds of busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably post something like, fine, it's a better calculator, I still love it. I use it every day for cut lists and for learning joints, so I'd defend it a bit. But I'd also say the climate work matters more than the AI arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I'd hoped AI would help me catch up faster on the skills I'm missing. My carpentry is behind where it should be, I'm still slow and I still botch mitres. But for my job and money, nothing much changes, and the retrofit work is booked for a year ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Fernleaf and keep using the AI for cut lists and for asking it to explain joints at night. I'd buy my co-op share this spring, which costs two thousand from my savings and makes me a full member with a vote. And I'd do Tomasz's Saturday window class he runs for apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, with a bit of impatience about my own skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a full member with a vote mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm not just an employee, I own a slice of the place and get a say in who we hire and what we charge. That's important to me politically, I don't think workers should just rent their labour to someone. At the last meeting we voted to pay apprentices the same day rate after a year, and I want to be in that room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your mitres let you down. What does that look like on a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I cut the window boards for a house on Linden Street and two of the corners had a gap you could slide a coin into. Tomasz didn't shout, he just handed me a new board and stood there while I did it again. I filmed my second try at the window boards and asked the AI app what I'd done wrong, and it spotted that my saw was drifting.

say: I'd call AI a **better calculator** and still **defend** it, since I use it daily.
I'd say **climate work** matters more than the AI arguments.
think: I'd be a bit **disappointed**, as I hoped AI would help me **catch up** faster.
For my **job and money** nothing changes, with retrofit work booked a year ahead.
do: Keep using AI for **cut lists** and for learning **joints** at night.
Buy a **co-op share** for two thousand this spring to become a full member.
Join Tomasz's **Saturday window class** for apprentices.
feel: **Calm** and content, with some **impatience** about her own skills.

fieldNote: She uses AI as a **learning coach**, not to replace work, which fits her **adaptive** style.

steps.text: Keep using the AI app to plan cut lists and learn joints

Join the Saturday window class run by the lead carpenter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, use it for the boring parts, and then make sure the time saved goes to the workers, not just faster profits. At Fernleaf we'd actually get to vote on that, which is the whole point of a co-op. Online I'd be the annoying person posting about how ownership solves this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is fine, the AI barely touches cutting wood-fibre board. What worries me is Noor. Graphic design is exactly the writing and checking that AI takes over, and my girlfriend Noor has already lost two logo clients to cheap AI tools this year. If her income halves, our plans shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build Fernleaf a proper AI tool for the heat-loss surveys and quotes, because right now Tomasz spends Sunday nights doing them by hand. I'd put a bit more aside each month in case Noor's work dries up. And we'd probably push back the wedding we were thinking about for 2028, until her work settles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly, but for Noor more than me. I feel in control of my side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did Noor react to losing those logo clients?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She laughed it off at first, then I found her at two in the morning redoing her website. She's brilliant at hand lettering and painted signs, which a printer can't do on a shop window, so I've been nudging her that way. She thinks I'm being naive, that every client will go cheap. We have that argument about once a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd build the co-op an AI quoting tool. Doesn't that take work from somebody?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a co-op it takes the boring bit off Tomasz, and he's the one who'd vote on it. Nobody gets sacked because the office is three of us sharing the paperwork. That's the difference I keep going on about. In a normal firm, the same tool would probably cost Bev in the office her job.

say: Use AI for **boring parts**, but the saved time should go to **workers**.
Online I'd keep saying **ownership** is the answer, like in our co-op.
think: My own job is fine, since AI barely touches cutting **wood-fibre board**.
Noor's **design work** is exactly what this hits, and she's lost **two clients** already.
do: Build the co-op an **AI tool** for heat-loss surveys and quotes.
Put **more aside** each month in case Noor's income halves.
Push back the **wedding** planned for 2028 until Noor's work settles.
feel: **Anxious**, mostly for **Noor**, while feeling in control of her own side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a moment for public ownership and for workers owning the robots, not three tech firms. I'd be pushing for a basic income, honestly, and I'd say that out loud. At Fernleaf I'd call an emergency members' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Noor's design work basically ends in 2028, I think, and mine gets three more years before the robots can fit a timber window. My girlfriend Noor and I are two incomes in one house, both going within five years. My savings would carry us maybe two years, and I'd be thirty-one with half a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get Fernleaf to put money aside to buy one of the early building robots together, so we own it instead of a big contractor. I'd retrain into running and programming that kit, I'm the one who's already good with the apps. Noor and I would stop all big spending and put the wedding money into the savings pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm good at change, but this is two of us at once, and fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between the AI and the robots mean for Fernleaf?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our quotes, surveys, ordering and scheduling would be AI in 2028, so the office side shrinks straight away. Then we've got three years where houses still need people on scaffolding. I'd want us to use those three years to learn the robots before they arrive, so on day one we're operating them, not competing with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the conversation with Noor like that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quiet, I think. She'd say she told me so about clients going cheap, and she'd be right. I'd say we've got money and we've got time to plan, and she'd ask how long, and I'd say two years if we're careful. Then we'd probably both sit up too late on our laptops, which is what we do when we're scared.

say: This calls for **public ownership** and workers owning the **robots**.
I'd push for a **basic income** and call an emergency **co-op meeting**.
think: Noor's design ends around **2028**, and robots fit windows three years later.
**Two incomes** going within five years, with savings lasting about **two years**.
do: Get Fernleaf to save up and buy an early **building robot** together.
Retrain to **run and program** that kit, since I'm good with apps.
Stop **big spending** and move the **wedding money** into savings.
feel: **Alarmed**, because it's **two incomes** at once, and fast.
S2.quote: My girlfriend Noor and I are two incomes in one house, both going within five years.
fieldNote: She expects a **household earner** to lose her income first, which drives the **alarm**.
Her plan is **ownership** again: the co-op buys the robot rather than competing with it.
Even an adaptive person is shaken when **two incomes** are hit together.

steps.text: Get the co-op to save for an early building robot
Retrain to run and program the co-op's robot
Move the wedding money into the household savings pot
Call for a basic income and public ownership

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up something fair, like retraining money and worker ownership funds, and that if governments waste it, that's on them. I'd keep posting about co-ops, because it's the one model I've seen work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years plus three gets me to 2034, so about eight years of carpentry, enough to get good. Noor gets five years to move into hand lettering and signs, which she's already half doing. It's still scary, but we can both see the path, and I'd be thirty-five with real skills and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get Fernleaf to start a robot fund now, a bit of every job's profit, so by 2033 we can buy kit. I'd do an evening course in programming the machines, maybe two nights a week. And Noor and I would actually get married in 2028 like we planned, because there'd be time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a manageable kind. More like nerves before an exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why go ahead with the wedding in this picture but not the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because five years means Noor can shift her work while she's still earning, rather than after it's gone. We'd keep it small, maybe thirty people in her parents' garden. I don't want to pause my whole life every time a tech company announces something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does an evening course in programming the machines look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably something online at first, then a proper one at the college once the robots exist. I already use AI every day to learn joints, so learning it to tell a robot what to cut feels like the next step. I know I'm still below average at the actual carpentry, so maybe this is where I end up better than the others.

say: **Five years** is enough to set up retraining money and **ownership funds**.
If governments **waste the time**, that's on them, and I'd keep posting about co-ops.
think: About **eight years** of carpentry gives me time to get good before robots.
Noor gets **five years** to move into hand lettering and signs while still earning.
do: Set up a Fernleaf **robot fund** from a slice of every job's profit.
Take an **evening course** in programming site machines two nights a week.
Go ahead with a **small wedding** in 2028 in Noor's parents' garden.
feel: **Anxious**, but manageable, like **nerves** before an exam.
S3.quote: I don't want to pause my whole life every time a tech company announces something.
fieldNote: Extra time lets Noor **shift while earning**, which changes the couple's plans most.
She sees **machine programming** as a place her weak hand skills matter less.
Her **co-op robot fund** idea shows long-range planning at a young age.

steps.text: Set up a co-op robot fund from every job's profit
Take a two-night-a-week course in programming site machines
Hold a small wedding in 2028 as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make sure working people own a share of this, through co-ops, unions and public funds. If we can't sort it in a decade, we've failed on purpose. I'd be at every meeting, probably making a nuisance of myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, with robots around 2039 I'd be forty, with twelve years of carpentry and probably running jobs. That feels fine to me, maybe even exciting. Noor would have ten years to change direction, which is a whole career's worth for a designer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Fernleaf and get really good, then train as a retrofit coordinator, the person who plans the whole job, using AI tools. I'd buy a second co-op share when I can. Noor and I would look at buying a house with my café money, which we'd been putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. It's far enough away that I can make it work for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Retrofit coordinator is planning work, and AI takes thinking jobs first. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point, and I know that. I'd see it as a role that runs the AI and the people together, not a role that writes the reports by hand. Maybe by 2036 it's half the size, but someone still has to stand in a cold kitchen and tell an elderly woman what's happening to her house. I'd be good at that bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a house, why then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The café money's been in the index fund doing nothing useful for us. With ten years of steady work ahead, a mortgage feels sensible, and Noor wants a room with a window to draw in. I'd want a wreck, honestly, a cold old terrace I could retrofit myself at weekends.

say: With **ten years**, working people should own a **share** through co-ops and public funds.
If we can't sort it in a decade, we've **failed on purpose**.
think: By **2039** I'd be forty, with twelve years of carpentry, which feels almost **exciting**.
Noor gets **ten years** to change direction, a whole career for a designer.
do: Get good at the trade, then train as a **retrofit coordinator** using AI tools.
Buy a **second co-op share** when I can.
Buy a **cold old terrace** with Noor and retrofit it at weekends.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly **hopeful**, since it's far enough to plan for.
S4.quote: Someone still has to stand in a cold kitchen and tell an elderly woman what's happening to her house.
fieldNote: She knew **coordination** is thinking work AI hits, and argued for the **human** part of it.
A decade **reduces** the household risk, because Noor can retrain while earning.
Her plans turn **long term**: a second share, a house and a career step.

steps.text: Train as a retrofit coordinator after getting good at carpentry
Buy a second co-op share when savings allow
Buy an old terrace with Noor and retrofit it at weekends

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Noor and I would both be hit within a few years of each other. What would help is public money for worker co-ops to buy robots, so small outfits like Fernleaf own the machines instead of being wiped out by contractors who can afford them first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the climate. Old houses still need insulating whatever happens with AI, and if robots can do the insulating faster, great. I just want the people who live in those houses, and the people who used to do the work, to share in it.

headlineQuote: Old houses still need insulating whatever happens with AI, and if robots can do the insulating faster, great.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old first-year carpenter** at a retrofit worker co-op, still slow with mitres.
Money from selling a **café share** sits in an index fund, giving her a **strong cushion**.
She uses **AI every day** to learn and plan, and wants workers to **own** the robots.
Her real risk is **Noor**, her freelance designer girlfriend, whose work AI hits first.
Her mood moves from **calm** to **alarmed** in the fast picture, easing as warning time grows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when she and Noor would both lose **income** within a few years.
whatWouldHelp: **Public money** for worker co-ops to buy robots, so small firms own the **machines**.
